newsitem.title: UK: Entrepreneur Goldsmith reopens British Euro fight.
newsitem.headline: Entrepreneur Goldsmith reopens British Euro fight.

text.p: Billionaire Sir James Goldsmith on Thursday called for British voters to be asked at a referendum whether they want to stay part of the European Union, reopening a political battle which has split the ruling Conservatives.

In full-page newspaper advertisements, Goldsmith, head of the Referendum Party, said voters should be given a choice between staying in what he termed a federal Europe or returning to the "common market" bloc of the 1970s and early 1980s.

The adverts set out for the first time the actual question Goldsmith wants put to voters. His new party has attracted support from right-wing Conservative voters worried at Brussels' hold over British affairs and fearful of further integration.
Goldsmith's clarification of his demands sparked sharp reactions from leading Conservatives.

"It's wind and fury and it's certainly irrelevant to the choice which faces the British electorate in the next six months," Health Secretary Stephen Dorrell told the BBC. Britain faces an election by May.
Former Conservative minister David Mellor, who faces a direct challenge from Goldsmith in his London constituency of Putney at the election, said: "He's appealing to the guts rather than the brain."

Denying he was running scared, Mellor told a BBC interviewer: "Anyone who approaches Sir James using the brain to think with will be very sceptical of a man who has flip-flopped over this subject far more than any politician."

But Goldsmith, who used his vast wealth to found the Referendum Party just two years ago, denied accusations he had been inconsistent. "I have not flip-flopped. Let the people decide whether they want to pull out," he told the BBC.

Both the Conservatives and the opposition Labour Party, which is far ahead in opinion polls, have promised in recent months to hold a referendum on whether or not Britain should enter a European single currency, due to be set up in 1999.
Goldsmith said on Thursday the single currency was only part of the issue, which was really whether Britons wanted a permanent transfer of sovereignty to European institutions.

His advert said voters should be asked: "Do you want the UK to be part of a federal Europe or do you want the UK to return to an association of sovereign nations that are part of a common trading market?"

The Conservatives are worried candidates put up by Goldsmith in the general election could siphon off support and hand vital seats to Labour. Goldsmith has promised to dissolve his party once a referendum on Britain's future in Europe takes place.
Labour leader Tony Blair has said he needs a six percent swing to his party to take power, ending 17 years of Conservative rule. Polls currently give him a 20 point lead.
